text: A one-page website for "Brew Lab", a small specialty coffee shop in Indiranagar, Bengaluru.Visitors should see the menu with prices, the opening hours, and where to find us, and be able to pre-order a coffee for pickup. It should feel warm and modern and work well on a phone. Include a section about our beans and the farms they come from, and a simple loyalty-card explainer (buy 9, get the 10th free).

@CEO I need three decisions before I can write a checkable charter. The brief leaves open how pre-order works without a backend, what to do about facts only the shop owner has, and how much of the site's goal is conversion versus brand story. My recommended pick is stated in each question.
1. Pre-order mechanism. The site is a single static file with no server, so it cannot take payment or store orders. Option A (recommended): the form builds a pre-filled order message and opens WhatsApp (or email) to the shop, with pay-at-pickup. Cost: zero, reversible, but needs a shop WhatsApp number and a person reading messages. Option B: a form that only shows an on-screen confirmation and sends nothing. Cost: looks finished but orders go nowhere, which is a risk to customers and the shop's reputation. Choose A or B?
2. Unverified facts. Menu items and prices, opening hours, address, WhatsApp number and farm names are known only to the Requester. Option A (recommended): build with clearly marked placeholder values, hold the 'done' verdict until the Requester confirms or replaces them, and never invent farm names or sourcing claims. Cost: one Requester round trip. Option B: ship plausible invented content as a draft. Cost: faster, but a real shop could publish false prices or false sourcing claims. Choose A or B?
3. Primary goal and trade-off. Should the charter rank the page's job as (A, recommended) 'get a phone visitor to a pre-order in as few taps as possible', with story sections (beans, farms, loyalty) kept compact below the order flow, or (B) 'brand story first', with ordering as one section among equals? A moves conversion and fits a mobile-first brief; B favors brand feel but may bury the order action. Choose A or B?

@Identity I chose A on all three, because each is the cheapest path that keeps the shop safe and the order action easy to reach.
1. 1. A. The form builds a pre-filled order message and opens WhatsApp (email as fallback), pay at pickup. Option B would show a confirmation while orders go nowhere, which harms customers and the shop. The brief is silent on the mechanism, so I picked the simplest working one. The WhatsApp number is an open input for the Requester, shown as a marked placeholder.
2. 2. A. Menu items and prices, hours, address, WhatsApp number and farm names are marked placeholders on the site, and no farm names or sourcing claims are invented. These are tracked as open inputs for the Requester and do not block done. The done-when list alone decides done, and the site must show the placeholders clearly so none can go live unnoticed.
3. 3. A. The charter ranks the page's job as getting a phone visitor to a pre-order in as few taps as possible. The beans and farms section and the loyalty explainer (buy 9, get the 10th free) stay compact below the order flow. The accepted trade-off is a little less room for brand story. The warm, modern feel comes from the visual design, not from section length.

@Adaptation the charter is recorded with order-first as the page's job, per the CEO's three decisions. Propose workflows that close the done-when items, and keep every Requester-only fact as a visibly marked placeholder.

proposal.name: Add pre-order form with WhatsApp and email fallback
proposal.goal_gap: Page has no way to pick items, enter a name and pickup time, or send an order. Done-when needs a form that opens wa.me with a mailto fallback and states that payment is at pickup.
proposal.expected_outcome: Order form placed before beans and loyalty in source order. It has item pickers fed from the menu, a name field, a pickup time field and a 'payment at pickup' line. JS builds a pre-filled message and opens a wa.me link to a marked placeholder number, with a mailto link as fallback. No payment fields and no text claiming the order was placed.

proposal.completion_check: File contains a form with item selection, a name input and a pickup time input, each at least 44px tall. The text 'payment at pickup' is present. The form precedes the beans and loyalty sections in source order.
